3.definition: 'The Magnificent' — the nickname that stuck to Lorenzo de' Medici, who dominated Florence 1469–1492 and whose household patronage of Botticelli, Pico, Poliziano, and the young Michelangelo produced the cultural moment the High Renaissance inherited.

'The Unfortunate' (more literally 'the foolish') — the dynastic nickname for Piero de' Medici, Lorenzo the Magnificent's son, who mismanaged the 1494 French crisis so badly that an angry Florentine mob drove the Medici into exile.

5.definition: Nicolosia Bellini, daughter of the painter Jacopo Bellini and sister of Gentile and Giovanni Bellini; her marriage to the Paduan painter Andrea Mantegna helped channel Florentine perspective and classical archaeology into the Venetian-Paduan visual world.

Arabic, 'house of manufacture' — the etymological root of the word 'arsenal,' borrowed into Venetian for the state shipyard whose prefabricated, sequential galley assembly anticipated the industrial assembly line by three centuries.

In Titian's output, the group of large mythological paintings — the Bacchus and Ariadne, the Venus of Urbino, the late Diana and Actaeon and Diana and Callisto for Philip II — that adapted classical myth to a Venetian erotic-poetic mood, painted with the same seriousness earlier artists reserved for biblical subjects.

Across the Renaissance the freestanding painted portrait emerged as a distinct prestige genre — the sitter in three-quarter pose, in rich dress, in a calm psychological register against a neutral or atmospheric ground — perfected by Bellini, Raphael, and above all Titian, who painted more European royalty than any other Renaissance figure.

The other great Venetian Renaissance achievement alongside painting: the polychoral style pioneered at San Marco by the Gabrielis, with separated choirs producing stereophonic spatial effects, which fed directly into the early opera of Monteverdi and the Baroque concertos of Vivaldi.

Giovanni Gabrieli’s 1597 collection of polychoral motets and instrumental canzonas for San Marco — the most famous monument of the Venetian polychoral style, whose spatially separated choirs and instrumental groups influenced composers across seventeenth-century Europe.

Silver mined at Potosí in the Andes from 1545 flowed through Manila to China and through Seville to Europe, restructuring global monetary relationships in ways that progressively disadvantaged the Mediterranean trading economies — including Venice — that had financed the Renaissance.

6.definition: The Latin Vulgate's rendering of the Greek 'metanoeite' in Matthew 4:17 — 'do penance' — which the medieval Church used to ground the sacrament of penance; Erasmus's 1516 retranslation to 'repent' (resipiscite) undermined that textual basis.

Erasmus's 1516 retranslation of the Greek 'metanoeite' in Matthew 4:17 — 'be of changed mind, repent' — replacing the Vulgate's 'poenitentiam agite' ('do penance') and so removing a key scriptural support for the Catholic sacrament of penance.

Latin, 'whose realm, his religion' — the principle established by the 1555 Peace of Augsburg under which each German prince chose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his own territory and his subjects had to follow, the structural template for European religious accommodation.

Erasmus's three years in Italy (1506–1509), spent at the peak of the High Renaissance working with Aldus Manutius on the Aldine classical editions; he left unimpressed by the moneymaking ecclesiastical institutions and never returned, and the satirical anti-clerical work that followed 'laid the egg that Luther hatched.'

8.definition: By the late sixteenth century every serious northern European painter or architect was expected to spend several years in Italy — usually based in Rome with side trips to Florence, Venice, and Naples — studying the masters and the Roman antiquities; the convention continued through the eighteenth-century Grand Tour and into the nineteenth century.

The third mechanism by which the Italian Renaissance spread across Europe: the systematic publication of Italian art treatises, architectural manuals, classical editions, and engraved reproductions of Italian masterworks that transmitted Italian knowledge without requiring travel.

Italian-language renderings of Greek and Roman classical texts that circulated across sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe, one of the channels through which the Italian Renaissance humanist recovery of antiquity reached readers who could not read Latin or Greek.

Printed engravings of major Italian paintings and sculptures — pioneered by Italian printmakers like Marcantonio Raimondi in the early sixteenth century, then taken up by northern print houses — that put images of Italian masterworks in the hands of artists across Europe who could not visit Italy.
